queue.recognise: A vast, wide-spreading pohutukawa with twisting limbs beside the school, with a carved red and white sign in front of it.
queue.story:
The sign beside this pohutukawa gives it a name, Te Waha o Rerekohu, the mouth of Rerekohu, and says the local school is named after it. Rerekohu was an ancestor of the people of this district. The sign sets out his line of descent and gives two accounts of how the tree got its name, one about a house that stood beside it and food brought as tribute to feed the child Rerekohu.

It puts the tree at well in excess of 350 years old and 40 metres across at its widest, and calls it reputed to be the largest of its species in the world. The New Zealand Herald describes it as nearly 40 metres wide and almost 20 metres high. The reader who sent the photograph puts it at 600 years, by their estimate,
queue.name: Pohutukawa
queue.note: The Te Waha O Rerekohu tree is believed to be the oldest and largest pohutukawa in the world.

queue.recognise: A massive, hollow, many-stemmed lime on a terrace with a low stone wall and a bench, looking out over Lake Neuchatel.
queue.story:
On a terrace above Lake Neuchatel in Estavayer-le-Lac, a lime has grown into something that hardly looks like a single tree. The trunk has split and healed around its own hollows, and several stems have twisted round each other into a cluster of ridges and knots. Roots grip the gravel like fingers.

Its age rests on tradition. A publication of the canton of Fribourg puts its planting around 1474, and local legend links it to the Battle of Morat in 1476. A tourist guide gives only the sixteenth century. Either way the tree is some four and a half to five and a half centuries old, and nobody has counted rings.

queue.recognise: A single enormous, straight, deeply ridged tulip tree trunk beside the Bear Creek trail, with a railing and steps down to it.
queue.story:
The Gennett Poplar is a tulip tree, which is neither a poplar nor a tulip, and it stands at the end of a short walk up Bear Creek in the north Georgia mountains. The trail starts at the end of a two-mile gravel road. After a little over half a mile it reaches a railing with steps down to the tree.

Hiking guides call it the second largest tree in Georgia, and one puts it at over 300 years old and more than 100 feet tall. Another gives its trunk as about 18 feet round at eye level, which is the figure we use for girth. queue.name: The Gennet Poplar (Tulip Tree)

queue.recognise: A huge, multi-stemmed old oak behind a low fence, with an information board and a bench in front of it, off the Bolderwood Ornamental Drive.
queue.story:
The Knightwood Oak is the biggest oak in the New Forest, about 7.4 metres round, and has been called the Queen of the Forest since Victorian times, when visiting it became a thing to do. The New Forest National Park Authority describes it as a fine example of an ancient pollard, a tree whose crown was cut back at head height so that it would keep sprouting new wood. Wikipedia says it was pollarded when about 200 years old and probably last cut in the middle of the nineteenth century.

queue.tree_name: A Cedar of the Meares Island Big Tree Trail
queue.recognise: A very wide redcedar with two trunks joined at a flared, buttressed base, beside the boardwalk on the Big Tree Trail.
queue.story:
On Meares Island, across the water from Tofino, a boardwalk threads through old-growth rainforest where western redcedars grow so large that two people with outstretched arms cannot reach round one. Tourism pages describe the trail's cedars as up to 1,500 years old, and the best known tree on it, the Hanging Garden Tree, is given a circumference of about 18.3 metres. We do not know which of the big cedars this reader's photograph shows, and no age has been measured for it, so we give none.

queue.tree_name: The Red Gum of Overbury Drive
queue.recognise: A big river red gum standing in the middle of the road on Overbury Drive, with the street curving around its trunk.
queue.story:
On Overbury Drive in Clarence Park, a quiet suburban street in Adelaide's inner south, a river red gum stands in the middle of the road and the tarmac bends around it. Press reports put it at about 200 years old and more than 20 metres tall. Residents call it the Sacred Tree, and it has become a symbol of holding out against urban spread.

Its position is the reason it is known. The photograph, taken at sunset, shows the pale, deeply furrowed trunk rising from the centre of the carriageway with power lines crossing in front and houses, parked cars and a few neighbours on either side. The crown spreads wide and green above it.

queue.tree_name: The Giant Sequoias of the Tall Trees Trail
queue.recognise: Two very tall, red-barked conifers with narrow crowns flanking a grass track, with a Douglas fir between them, on the Tall Trees Trail.
queue.story:
Two giant sequoias stand either side of the track on the Tall Trees Trail beside the Rhinefield Ornamental Drive, and from the path they look as if they belong to a different forest. A Waymarking listing says they were planted in 1859 as part of the Rhinefield estate, which would make them about 165 years old, and calls them the heaviest and tallest trees in the New Forest National Park. That is a hobbyist claim, not a survey.

The only measurement we found is a girth of 9.41 metres for one of them, taken in October 2019 and reported on a redwood enthusiasts' site. Estimates of their height range from about 30 to 45 metres and come from visitors with no instruments, so we give none.

queue.tree_name: The Great Ginkgo of Hida Kokubunji
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by aerial roots hanging like breasts, the reason it is called Chichi Icho, with stone jizo statues at its base, 10 metres round. It stands between the main hall and bell tower gate of Hida Kokubunji.
queue.story:
When this ginkgo drops its last leaf, Hida expects its first snow the next day. The town treats it as its own herald of winter. It stands between the main hall and the bell-tower gate of Hida Kokubunji, roughly ten metres round and 27 to 28 metres tall. Sources put its age between 1,200 and 1,300 years, the temple claiming the higher figure and the prefecture the lower. By the temple's own account the monk Gyoki planted it in 737, when Hida Kokubunji was founded by decree of Emperor Shomu.
